claims.claim: Carbohydrates are one of the six nutrient classes (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water, vitamins, minerals), and the standard working definition is that they are molecules made of sugar units.

The body breaks carbohydrates down into glucose, which is the main source of energy for the body's cells, tissues, and organs; glucose can be used immediately or stored in the liver and muscles for later use.
Glucose is the preferred fuel for the brain and nervous system, and circulating glucose is the first source of energy used during activity.

When carbohydrate and fat meet the body's energy needs, dietary protein is spared for its own jobs such as tissue repair and restoration, rather than being burned as fuel (the protein-sparing effect).
Carbohydrate provides about 4 calories per gram of energy, per the USDA & HHS Dietary Guidelines 2020-2025 as tabulated in OpenStax nutrition texts.

The three broad forms of carbohydrate are sugars, starches, and fiber: sugars are the most basic form, starches are made of many sugar units strung together that the body digests, and fiber is a plant carbohydrate that the body cannot fully digest.
Carbohydrate-rich foods come from fruits, grains (bread, rice, cereals, pasta), dairy (milk, yogurt), legumes (dried beans, lentils, peas), and starchy vegetables such as potatoes and corn.
Lactose, the natural sugar found in milk and dairy products, is a carbohydrate made of two sugar units (glucose and galactose).

Carbohydrate quality matters more than carbohydrate presence: whole and minimally processed sources (whole grains, vegetables, fruits, beans) deliver fiber, vitamins, and minerals, while highly processed and refined sources such as sodas, white bread, and pastries deliver sugar units with little else and are associated with worse health outcomes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Simple-versus-complex framing: MedlinePlus classifies sugars as 'simple carbohydrates' and starches and fiber as 'complex carbohydrates,' while other sources treat carbohydrate quality as a spectrum rather than two clean buckets.
positions: MedlinePlus: sugars are simple carbohydrates; starches and fiber are complex carbohydrates.
Harvard Nutrition Source and current dietary guidance emphasize a quality continuum from whole to refined/processed sources.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson names the three forms (sugars, starches, fiber) and does not teach the simple-versus-complex framework, which belongs to the sibling topic nutrition:foundations:simple-and-complex-carbohydrates.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Recommended share of calories from carbohydrate: MedlinePlus reports 45-65% of calories (the AMDR), while OpenStax Nutrition for Nurses states 50-65%.
positions: MedlinePlus: 45 to 65% of calories from carbohydrate on average.
OpenStax Nutrition for Nurses 2.1: carbohydrates should make up 50-65% of caloric intake.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson omits the percentage entirely, so the discrepancy does not surface in the content; energy recommendations belong to the sibling topic nutrition:foundations:energy-and-calories.
